The spousal RRSP withdrawal calendar: review the year of withdrawal and the two before it

Use four graphics to organize a contributor’s annual record, follow a moving calendar window and distinguish elapsed months from income-reporting decisions.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original hypothetical calendar ledger using CRA’s general spousal-RRSP calendar-year review described in the cited public guidance, reviewed 25 October 2026. The amounts aggregate one contributor’s deposits to the same annuitant’s RRSPs across the entered years; they are not the annuitant’s own deposits, investment returns, contribution room, deductions or transfers. Each review totals the withdrawal calendar year and the two preceding calendar years. Totals identify records to review; they are not attributed income or tax payable. No withdrawal amount, prior attribution, income allocation, final tax, withholding, account eligibility, relationship exception, residency exception, RRIF minimum, SPP or FHSA transfer is calculated. Future dates are examples conditional on the reviewed rule, not a promise that future law will stay unchanged. The separate 2026 example date remains a date illustration even when its annual deposit amount is zero. Month gaps compare month labels without day-of-month precision. A calendar window alone does not establish a tax-free or permitted withdrawal.

The central idea

Calendar dates help identify which contribution records need review. Determining who reports a withdrawal also requires the applicable tax process and the full relevant history.

01

Identify the contributor and the annuitant before drawing the calendar

A spousal or common-law partner RRSP involves two roles. The contributor makes deposits for the other person’s plan, while the annuitant is the person entitled to receive the plan amounts. A useful withdrawal review keeps those roles and the relevant records clear before discussing a tax result.

The annual inputs in this tool represent one contributor’s deposits to the same annuitant’s RRSPs across calendar years. They are hypothetical totals, not contribution-room estimates or instructions to make deposits. The annuitant’s own contributions are a separate history and are not silently added to this contributor’s ledger.

CRA’s spousal-RRSP withdrawal guidance describes circumstances in which a contributor may report some or all of a withdrawal. The article explains the calendar component of that review without calculating anyone’s income allocation.

02

Build the window from calendar-year labels

The reviewed CRA framework considers the withdrawal year and the two preceding calendar years. If the hypothetical withdrawal is in 2029, the displayed review covers 2027, 2028 and 2029. For a 2028 withdrawal, the three labels become 2026, 2027 and 2028.

The stacked bars apply that arithmetic to the same entered annual record. Each colour shows one relative year in the review. The bar total is a sum of contribution records to examine. It is not a calculation of attributed income, because no withdrawal amount or full attribution history is supplied to this tool.

The controls cover 2025–2031 so every displayed three-year window is complete within the illustration. For an actual review, gather the relevant records across plans rather than looking only at the account from which money will be withdrawn. Verify the applicable rules and tax-year process before acting on a future-date example.

03

Read the month gap without replacing the calendar rule

A deposit in December 2026 and an example withdrawal in January 2029 are 25 month labels apart. Yet the 2029 review labels are 2027, 2028 and 2029, which exclude 2026. Moving the example deposit to January 2026 makes the elapsed gap 36 months while leaving the same calendar-year membership.

The reverse comparison also matters. A December 2026 deposit and a December 2028 withdrawal are 24 month labels apart, and 2026 remains inside the 2026–2028 review. The amount of time between two dates and the three calendar years selected by the rule should therefore be recorded as separate facts.

The calculation is 12 × (withdrawal year − contribution year) + withdrawal month − contribution month. It uses month labels rather than exact days. The fixed matrix compares several 2026 deposit months with several 2029 withdrawal months, while the bar chart uses the months selected in the controls.

04

A later contribution can change the relevant record set

The default ledger has CAD 5,000 in 2026 and zero in the other years. The 2027 and 2028 windows include that recorded amount. The 2029 window does not. This is an example of selecting records by year; a zero bar should not be interpreted as a complete tax conclusion.

Now enter CAD 2,000 for 2028. The 2029 window includes that later amount even though it still excludes 2026. Focusing on the date of the earliest deposit would miss the newer record. The graph keeps each year separate so that the later contribution is visible.

These future annual amounts are planning assumptions. A real review uses deposits actually made and the complete relevant history. The calendar-year ledger is also separate from the year for which a contribution deduction may be claimed. Keep the deposit receipt date rather than inferring it from a deduction on a return.

05

Use the calendar as the start of the income-reporting review

CRA provides Form T2205 for determining the income amounts the contributor and annuitant must report in the applicable circumstances. Its published worked example considers a withdrawal and contribution history together. A window total on its own is therefore insufficient to allocate a withdrawal between people.

This tool does not model earlier withdrawals or attribution, relationship or residency exceptions, RRIF minimums, specified pension plans or FHSA transfers. It also calculates no withholding or final tax. Those matters should be checked in the applicable current process rather than inferred from the date graphics.

For the household cash plan, separately record the gross withdrawal, immediate proceeds, any tax allowance and when the money is required. Read the withholding guide for that distinction. The calendar can improve the record review while the withdrawal’s legal, reporting and cash consequences remain distinct planning questions.
